title: LabPrism
description: Inspect lab observations with their original units, dates and source reference text. LabPrism keeps normalized record fields available beside readable results.
attribution: Built on the FinchNode production API.
workflow: Switch between lab observations, inspect source-provided reference text, and examine the exact FHIR resource and diagnostic report. No historical trend is invented.
subject: Lab result viewer & source detail inspector
label: Inside the observation
headline: A lab result is more than a number
summary: How LabPrism keeps units, dates, reference text and normalized fields beside a result without inventing an interpretation.
sections: LabPrism is a viewer for the observations returned in an authorized record. It keeps a result beside its supplied name, unit, date and reference text. These fields are separate parts of the record. Combining them into a single score would hide useful detail, so the interface lets the visitor select an observation and inspect its individual fields.

If a source supplies reference information, the viewer preserves it as context for that observation. It does not create a universal reference range or turn a value into a diagnosis. A missing unit or date remains missing. Questions about meaning, comparisons between laboratories, or whether a result needs action require professional interpretation beyond this interface.
Why there is no invented trend

A line chart implies repeated measurements on a comparable basis. A single returned observation cannot establish that history. LabPrism therefore emphasizes inspection of available observations rather than synthesizing a time series. Even when several entries are present, their names, units and dates deserve review before a visitor assumes they represent the same measurement.

Our integration uses FinchNode to obtain authorized normalized records through a server connection. The inspection panel shows the returned normalized JSON and available diagnostic report information. It is not a guarantee that the untouched upstream FHIR bundle is present. Keeping this boundary visible helps a developer or curious visitor understand which representation they are actually reading.

Production activation is pending, so the deployed viewer does not yet establish a successful live connection. Once enabled, returned categories and sync warnings still determine what is available. The public repository explains the observation viewer, connection adapter and category restrictions. The purpose is readable source context, with medical interpretation left to the care team.
guideIntro: Learn to inspect a lab entry as a complete record: result text, unit, source reference information, status and the normalized fields behind the display.
finchnodeContext: LabPrism builds its result inspector around lab entries returned through FinchNode. The interface keeps supplied units, reference text and missing-field states visible so that a normalized display is not mistaken for a clinical interpretation.

articles.title: How to inspect a lab result’s fields in LabPrism
articles.description: Find the value, unit, source reference text and status behind a lab entry, and inspect the normalized observation without inventing missing information.

sections.heading: Select the exact entry
paragraphs: The result list shows a label and the date available to the app. Select the entry you want to inspect before comparing details. Similar labels do not establish that two observations used the same method or should be treated as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Read the value together with its context
paragraphs: The selected panel displays the result quantity, status, source reference text and any supplied interpretation. Read these together instead of copying the number alone. LabPrism does not generate a replacement reference range when the source omits one.
items: Check the selected label and available code.
Keep the unit beside any numerical value you discuss.
Distinguish source interpretation from your own question about it.
Notice any field explicitly marked as not supplied.

sections.heading: Expand the normalized observation
paragraphs: The inspector below the panel exposes the returned object. Use it to check which field supports the display and whether additional context was returned. The object is the normalized representation used by this app, not a promise of the original lab report or every field in the source system.

sections.heading: Keep a route to the original report
paragraphs: If a value or field needs clarification, consult the original report and the appropriate care professional. The app does not diagnose conditions, recalculate laboratory ranges, or establish a historical trend. Public explanations are available now; live imports still depend on production activation.

questions.question: Why does a result have no reference range?
questions.answer: The returned entry may not contain one. LabPrism displays that absence instead of substituting a general range.

questions.question: Is the JSON panel the original laboratory document?
questions.answer: No. It shows the normalized entry supplied to the app, which can differ from the original document.

articles.title: Why LabPrism shows missing lab fields explicitly
articles.description: How LabPrism handles absent units, reference text and interpretation when displaying normalized lab entries from an authorized record connection.

sections.heading: Absence is part of the result display
paragraphs: A result inspector needs to distinguish a supplied value from an absent field. LabPrism uses explicit fallback text for missing reference information, interpretation and source details. A fallback label describes the display state; it is not a finding about the patient.

sections.heading: Do not make a more complete-looking record
paragraphs: The interface reads what was returned and leaves missing clinical context visible. It does not insert a familiar laboratory range or derive a diagnosis from the number. A polished presentation should still let a reader recognize where the available information ends.

sections.heading: Inspect the mapping when something looks unexpected
paragraphs: Developers can compare the selected normalized object with the displayed quantity and labels. That is a concrete debugging path: identify the field, check the formatting helper, and verify the fallback. It is more useful than treating every unexpected display as an upstream clinical error.

sections.heading: Separate software checks from interpretation
paragraphs: Implementation tests can check that an absent field remains absent and that source text survives formatting. They do not clinically validate a result. A future operator should keep that distinction when adding comparison features. The existing application has not activated live patient connections.

questions.question: Does normalization fill in every missing field?
questions.answer: The interface cannot assume it does. It handles the response it receives and exposes missing context explicitly.

finchnode.heading: The FinchNode normalization boundary
finchnode.text: LabPrism uses FinchNode as the upstream connection for its lab category. The product then chooses how to present returned fields and how to describe omissions. Readers can inspect that boundary through the visible JSON and the public implementation.
finchnode.label: FinchNode’s published API contract

articles.title: Why health AI needs lab context, not just result numbers
articles.description: LabPrism explores why units, reference text, status and missing fields shape the usefulness of patient data for future AI-assisted lab experiences.

sections.heading: The unit belongs in the input
paragraphs: A numerical result stripped of its unit is an incomplete input to a lab-oriented product. The test label, available code, source reference text and status can all change what a reader should ask next. A health startup therefore needs a plan for retaining record context before it adds a fluent explanation layer.

LabPrism’s existing inspector keeps the selected entry visible as both a readable panel and normalized JSON. That pairing is a useful starting point for identifying what any later summary actually had available to it.

sections.heading: AI can make information easier to navigate
paragraphs: A proposed assistant could help a user find a particular field, collect questions about an unfamiliar label or explain how to navigate the original report. Those tasks still need a route back to the exact source information. Generating a confident clinical interpretation from incomplete context would be a much larger claim.

The FDA describes both the potential of AI to draw insights from healthcare data and the need for good machine-learning practice across a product’s lifecycle. That is a useful reference for startup teams considering clinical functionality; it is not evidence that LabPrism has a validated clinical AI feature.

links.label: FDA overview of good machine-learning practice

sections.heading: Build an evaluation around missingness
paragraphs: Before choosing a model, define the behavior you want when a reference range, unit or interpretation is absent. A successful output may need to say what is missing and stop. Evaluation examples should include awkward cases, rather than only a complete and easy-to-read observation.
items: A value with no supplied unit.
A result with reference text but no interpretation.
Several similarly named entries from different sources.
An output that must point back to the selected record.

sections.heading: FinchNode connects the category; LabPrism preserves the boundary
paragraphs: LabPrism uses FinchNode in its source implementation for authorized lab records, then displays the normalized fields it receives. The app does not invent a reference range to make the panel look complete. That same discipline would matter if an operator later added AI-assisted navigation.

A structured API makes fields available to software; it does not guarantee that every field is present or clinically comparable. The selected object and its source context remain the evidence. Live patient imports still require production activation.

sections.heading: Patient data should narrow uncertainty, not hide it
paragraphs: The opportunity for a health startup is to make the record easier to inspect without erasing its limits. LabPrism currently does that through direct display and source-preserving fallbacks. Any AI addition should be judged against that baseline, with a clear statement of what it can and cannot establish.

questions.question: Does LabPrism generate diagnoses or AI lab interpretations?
questions.answer: No. It displays the result information and interpretation supplied in the returned record, where present.

questions.question: Will more data automatically make an AI feature reliable?
questions.answer: No. The data must be appropriate to the intended task, and the output still needs evaluation for errors, omissions and unsupported claims.
